title: Sanctions against PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP and Jonathan Hinchliffe
text:
Edited for publication

IN THE MATTER OF
THE EXECUTIVE COUNSEL OF THE FINANCIAL REPORTING COUNCIL
-and-
(1) PRICEWATERHOUSECOOPERS LLP
(2) JONATHAN HINCHLIFFE

FINAL SETTLEMENT DECISION NOTICE
Pursuant to Rule 108 of the Audit Enforcement Procedure

This Final Settlement Decision Notice is a document prepared by Executive
Counsel following an investigation relating to, and admissions made by, the
Respondents. It does not make findings against any persons other than the
Respondents and it would not be fair to treat any part of this document as
constituting or evidencing findings against any other persons since they are not
parties to the proceedings.

1.
INTRODUCTION
1.1. The Financial Reporting Council (the “FRC”) is the competent authority for statutory
audit in the UK and operates the Audit Enforcement Procedure (the “AEP”), revised in
June 2023. The AEP sets out the rules and procedure for the investigation,
prosecution and sanctioning of breaches of Relevant Requirements.
1.2. The AEP contains a number of defined terms and, for convenience, those defined
terms are also used within this document. Where defined terms are used, they appear
in italics.
1.3. This Final Settlement Decision Notice also uses the following definitions:

2

1.3.1.
“FY2019” means the financial year ended 30 April 2019, “FY2019 Financial
Statements” means the consolidated financial statements of Wyelands Bank
plc (the “Bank”) for that period, and “FY2019 Audit” means the statutory
audit of the FY2019 Financial Statements.
1.3.2.
“Respondents” means:
1.3.2.1. PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP (“PwC”), which was the Statutory
Audit Firm for the FY2019 Audit.
1.3.2.2. Jonathan Hinchliffe (“Mr Hinchliffe”), who was the Statutory Auditor
for the FY2019 Audit, and signed the FY2019 Audit report on behalf
of PwC on 26 July 2019.
1.4. In accordance with Rule 102 of the AEP, Executive Counsel entered into settlement
discussions with the Respondents.
1.5. A Proposed Settlement Decision Notice was issued by Executive Counsel on 26
September 2024 pursuant to Rule 103 of the AEP in relation to the conduct of the
Respondents in respect of the FY2019 Audit. The Respondents provided written
agreement to the Proposed Settlement Decision Notice, pursuant to Rule 105 of the
AEP, on 4 October 2024. The Convener subsequently appointed an Independent
Reviewer, pursuant to Rule 106 of the AEP, to consider the Proposed Settlement
Decision Notice.
1.6. On 18 October 2024, the Independent Reviewer approved the issuance of this Final
Settlement Decision Notice pursuant to Rule 107(a) of the AEP.
1.7. In accordance with Rule 108 of the AEP this Final Settlement Decision Notice sets out:
1.7.1.
The breaches of Relevant Requirements, with reasons;
1.7.2.
The Sanctions imposed on the Respondents, with reasons; and
1.7.3.
The amount payable in respect of Executive Counsel’s Costs.
1.8. This Final Settlement Decision Notice is divided into the following sections:
1.8.1.
Section 2: Executive Summary of the breaches of Relevant Requirements;
1.8.2.
Section 3: Background;
1.8.3.
Section 4: Relevant Requirements to which the breaches relate;
1.8.4.
Section 5: Detail of the breaches of Relevant Requirements;
1.8.5.
Section 6: Sanctions; and

3

1.8.6.
Section 7: Costs.
2.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF THE BREACHES OF RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS
2.1. As is set out in this Final Settlement Decision Notice, there were a number of failures
by the Respondents in the manner in which the FY2019 Audit was conducted. The
breaches of Relevant Requirements relate to six areas of audit work as set out below:
2.1.1.
Audit risk assessment:
2.1.1.1. Failing to: (i) adequately consider audit risks posed by the Bank’s
membership of the Gupta Family Group Alliance (the “GFG
Alliance”), and (ii) identify key developments relevant to the overall
assessment of risk, at the planning stage of the audit;
2.1.1.2. Failing to treat the risk around the completeness of related party
disclosures as elevated;
2.1.1.3. Failing to adequately consider: (i) the complexity of transactions with
members of the GFG Alliance, or (ii) whether they comprised
significant transactions with related parties, in concluding that the
risks identified at the financial statement and assertion levels were
appropriate;
2.1.1.4. Failing to revisit the risk assessment in respect of compliance with
laws and regulations, in light of correspondence from the Prudential
Regulation Authority (the “PRA”) in June and July 2019; and
2.1.1.5. Failing to revisit the risk assessment in respect of completeness of
related party disclosures, in light of a fee letter indicating that
management’s listing was incomplete.
2.1.2.
Audit of the Bank’s compliance with laws and regulations:
2.1.2.1. Failing to obtain all relevant PRA correspondence; and
2.1.2.2. Failing to react appropriately to the PRA correspondence that was
obtained.
2.1.3.
Audit of the Bank’s related parties and related party transactions:
2.1.3.1. Failing to perform sufficient risk assessment procedures to
understand the type and purpose of related party transactions;

4

2.1.3.2. Failing to document an understanding of management’s controls for
identifying, accounting for and disclosing related party transactions;
2.1.3.3. Failing to obtain and document sufficient appropriate audit evidence
about whether related party relationships and transactions had been
appropriately disclosed; and
2.1.3.4. Failing to exercise adequate professional skepticism in relation to the
refusal by management to disclose a quantitative measure of the
proportion of GFG Alliance introduced business.
2.1.4.
Audit of the Bank’s assessment of going concern:
2.1.4.1. Failing to have proper regard to the PRA’s concerns in the context of
going concern; and
2.1.4.2. Failing to properly challenge the assumptions underlying
management’s going concern assessment, and document the audit
judgments made.
2.1.5.
Audit of the Bank’s loans and advances:
2.1.5.1. Failing to carry out sufficient procedures to understand adequately
the Bank’s lending business; and
2.1.5.2. Failing to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to verify the
existence of some of the loans.
2.1.6.
Audit of the Bank’s provision for Expected Credit Loss (“ECL”):
2.1.6.1. Failing to adequately evaluate whether the “debt stacking”
assumption applied by the Bank was reasonable; and
2.1.6.2. Failing to apply sufficient professional skepticism to other aspects of
the Bank’s ECL approach.
2.2. Section 5 of this Final Settlement Decision Notice sets out the detailed breaches of
Relevant Requirements. This Final Settlement Decision Notice does not make a
finding that the FY2019 Financial Statements were misstated, except in relation to the
related party disclosures as described in Section 5 under Breach 3.
2.3. This Final Settlement Decision Notice sets out the following Sanctions imposed on the
Respondents:

5

2.3.1.
Against PwC:
2.3.1.1. A financial sanction of £4,500,000, adjusted for the mitigating factor
of exceptional co-operation by a reduction of 5% and further
discounted for admissions and early disposal by 32.5%, so that the
amount payable is £2,885,625;
2.3.1.2. A published statement in the form of a Severe Reprimand;
2.3.1.3. A Declaration that the FY2019 Audit report did not satisfy Relevant
Requirements, as set out in this Final Settlement Decision Notice;
2.3.1.4. An Order requiring PwC to take specified action with the aim of
preventing the recurrence of the breaches.
2.3.2.
Against Mr Hinchliffe:
2.3.2.1. A financial sanction of £55,000, adjusted for the mitigating factor of
exceptional co-operation by a reduction of 10% and further
discounted for admissions and early disposal by 32.5%, so that the
amount payable is £33,412;
2.3.2.2. A published statement in the form of a Severe Reprimand;
2.3.2.3. A Declaration that the FY2019 Audit report did not satisfy Relevant
Requirements, as set out in this Final Settlement Decision Notice.
3.
BACKGROUND
The Respondents
3.1. PwC is the largest audit firm in the UK, with total fee income of £4,139m in 2023 (the
latest year for which figures are available). Of this, £965m was derived from audit
work. In 2023 the firm had 995 partners in total, and 339 individuals qualified to act as
Statutory Auditors entitled to sign audit reports on the firm’s behalf.
3.2. Mr Hinchliffe joined PwC in 2002 and qualified as a Statutory Auditor in 2013. At the
time of the FY2019 Audit he was an employee of PwC, with the job title of Director. He
resigned from PwC and left in April 2024.
3.3. PwC was the Bank's Statutory Audit Firm for the financial years FY2015 to FY2019; for
the first two of these financial years the Bank was under different ownership and had a
different name, as described in paragraph 3.4 below. Mr Hinchliffe carried out the
Statutory Audits of the Bank’s financial statements for FY2015 to 2019, signing the
audit reports on behalf of PwC as Statutory Auditor.

6

The Bank
3.4. The Bank was incorporated in 1980 under a different name. In December 2016 it was
acquired (via two intermediate holding companies and a trust) by a new beneficial
owner (the “Shareholder”), and renamed Wyelands Bank plc. The Shareholder was
the owner (with a family member) of the GFG Alliance of global businesses operating
in a number of industries including steel, aluminium and renewable energy.
3.5. As a credit institution, the Bank was a Public Interest Entity (“PIE”) for statutory audit
purposes. The Bank was regulated by the PRA and the Financial Conduct Authority
from December 2016. The PRA designated the Bank as a Category 4 UK bank,
meaning that it was regarded as having very little capacity individually to cause
disruption to the UK financial system if it were to fail, but difficulties across the whole
sector or subsector had the potential to cause disruption.
3.6. By FY2019 the Bank's business was mainly in trade finance, predominantly in the
metals and commodities sectors and largely funded by deposits from retail customers.
It had grown this business very significantly in the two years since its acquisition by the
Shareholder, chiefly through business linked to the GFG Alliance. This was consistent
with the Regulatory Business Plan (“RBP”) that the Bank presented to the PRA in
2016, which stated that, in its early years, the Bank would source and support low risk
lending opportunities introduced by the GFG Alliance. However, the Bank’s 2018
Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (“ICAAP”) stated that, by April 2019,
the Bank aimed to reduce the proportion of GFG Alliance-introduced business to 65%.
Despite this, the Bank's management reported to its Audit Committee in March 2019
that 84% of the Bank's business was still being introduced by the GFG Alliance.
3.7. The Bank’s primary trade finance product was invoice discounting, which accounted
for £181.7m of the Bank’s total £437.7m loans and advances (before provisions). This
involved the Bank buying the debt owed by the buyer to the seller in relation to a sale
of goods or services (in other words, the invoice). The Bank would buy the invoice
from the seller at a discount, paying the seller the discounted sum immediately, and
would then collect the entire debt from the buyer on the invoice due date. The seller
would have the benefit of certain and early payment of the discounted sum, while the
Bank would profit to the extent of the discount (assuming the buyer paid the debt). In
many instances, the seller was a GFG Alliance member.
3.8. Also included in the Bank’s business were the following asset-based lending products
(the “Asset Based Lending Transactions”):

7

3.8.1.
Block finance loans totalling £31.6m, two of which related to blocks of
receivables purchased from two GFG Alliance members for £18m (the “Block
Finance Loans”). These loans operated in a similar way to invoice
discounting, as described in paragraph 3.7 above, but they related to multiple,
rather than individual, invoices. The sellers acted as collection agents for the
Bank.
3.8.2.
Loans totalling £104.9m to 13 special purpose vehicles (“SPVs”) engaged in
the development and operation of hydropower plants in the UK (the
“Hydropower Loans”). These loans were made primarily to refinance existing
indebtedness to other financiers. The SPVs were previously owned by a GFG
Alliance member but ownership was transferred to third parties at loan
issuance. It was intended that a GFG Alliance member would repurchase the
SPVs, and this transaction would include the repayment of the loans.
3.8.3.
Loans to a GFG Alliance member totalling £32.8m, related to invoices for
steel inventory sold to nine SPVs, where the Bank had retained title security
(the “Retained Title Loans”). While the loan was made to the GFG Alliance
member, the amounts due under the invoices were to be collected from the
SPVs.
3.8.4.
Inventory loans totalling £29.2m, two of which related to steel inventory
purchased by two SPVs from a GFG Alliance member for £27.3m (the
“Inventory Loans”). The loans were made to the SPVs and it was intended
that repayment of the loans would occur upon repurchase of the steel
inventory by the GFG Alliance member.
3.8.5.
Bridging loans totalling £39.9m, related to electricity generators purchased by
five SPVs from a GFG Alliance member (the “Bridging Loans”). While the
loans were made to the SPVs, the GFG Alliance member acted as their agent
in relation to the loans.
PRA correspondence prior to the commencement of work on the FY2019 Audit
3.9. The PRA noted in a letter to the Bank dated 8 March 2018 (the “March 2018 PRA
letter”) that, while the Bank had grown its balance sheet significantly over the
preceding 12 months and this demonstrated the viability of its business model, the
sustainability of the business remained unproven and would take longer to establish. It
was noted that the Bank was working actively to originate more of its own business, as

8

distinct from business sourced from GFG Alliance members. Establishing this
independence would be an important factor in the PRA’s assessment of sustainability.
3.10. The March 2018 PRA letter also reported issues with the Bank's monitoring of capital
adequacy, including data quality, reconciliation and reporting issues, which indicated a
cause for concern around governance. The PRA was concerned at signs that the
Board of the Bank was not challenging matters presented to it, and asked it to continue
to ensure the Bank's plans were not unduly influenced by the Shareholder.
3.11. The PRA raised further concerns in a letter to the Bank dated 12 July 2018 (the “July
2018 PRA letter”). While it acknowledged that the Bank was a new bank with
developing underwriting processes and credit risk management framework, the PRA
identified a number of key areas where development was needed to ensure that the
Bank undertook its business prudentially. It noted that the Bank's risk appetites lacked
granularity, its risk framework was not well-defined, and credit policies and procedures
also needed to be more clearly articulated. The PRA also noted that the total amount
of the Bank’s loans that were overdue exceeded 50% of the Bank's capital base at the
time of its review, and advised the Bank to ensure future late payments were identified
and monitored, and that the risk they posed to the Bank and its stability should be
mitigated.
The FY2019 Financial Statements and Audit
3.12. The FY2019 Financial Statements reported that the Bank and its subsidiaries had total
assets of £856.0m (FY2018: £604.5m), including loans and advances to customers of
£433.7m after provisions (FY2018: £299.1m) and cash and cash equivalents of
£232.8m (FY2018: £65.6m). Total liabilities of £734.3m were reported (FY2018:
£512.8m), including customer deposits of £726.6m (FY2018: £506.2m). The Bank and
its subsidiaries reported a pre-tax profit of £469,000 (FY2018: £39,000).
3.13. FY2019 was the first year in which the Bank had to apply the accounting standard
IFRS 9: Financial Instruments, which set out a new approach to calculating an
allowance for ECL. In the FY2019 Financial Statements the Bank recognised a
provision of £3.9m for ECL, representing 0.9% of the total loan balance.
3.14. The FY2019 Financial Statements stated that the Bank considered members of the
GFG Alliance to be related parties, but the only related party transactions reported with
GFG Alliance members were interest income of £1.2m and other income of £2.0m
(FY18: £3.9m and £0, respectively), and other assets of £0.9m and customer deposits
of £0.7m (FY18: £0 and £26.2m, respectively). The Annual Report stated that:

9

“During our first two years, our rapid growth and strong financial performance has
owed much to our ability to source business through introductions from companies
controlled by our shareholder. This business has been undertaken on commercial
terms, frequently in competition with other banks. Our approach is to treat
shareholder-introduced clients in the same way that we would treat any other
customer.”
3.15. The Annual Report also stated that a goal of the Bank had been to do business with a
wider base of clients, and it aimed in future years to broaden its customer base both in
absolute terms and as a proportion of its business. The Annual Report noted that over
the year the Bank had continued to develop new business streams through Trade
Finance, Asset Based Lending and Asset Finance to third parties.
3.16. In June 2019, while the FY2019 Audit was being carried out, the PRA wrote to the
Bank (the “June 2019 PRA Letter”) giving notice that the Bank had been placed on
the PRA’s watchlist due to concerns including the Bank's reliance on GFG Alliance
companies, a potential breach of large exposure rules, the sustainability of its business
model and the nature and quality of its loan book. The PRA described this watchlist as
a list of firms that the PRA was most concerned about from the perspective of its
statutory objectives.
3.17. On 22 July 2019, the PRA issued a notice under section 166 of the Financial Services
and Markets Act 2000 (the “s.166 Requirement Notice”) requiring the Bank to obtain
a skilled person's report (the “s.166 review”). The report was required to review: (i) the
Bank's exposure in relation to the Hydropower Loans against the large exposure rules
in the Capital Requirements Regulation and guidelines on connected clients, and (ii)
the Bank's procedures for determining large exposures and regulatory reporting, and
to provide a view on the effectiveness of those procedures. The PRA was concerned
that the Hydropower Loans exposures were to parties constituting a “group of
connected counterparties” for the purposes of calculating the Bank's large exposure
risk for capital purposes, on the basis that they were connected to each other. The
PRA also made reference to the degree of influence exercised by GFG Alliance
members and their relationship with the counterparties, and the role of the Bank’s
board and senior executives in ensuring that loans complied with connected client and
related party rules.
3.18. On 26 July 2019, Mr Hinchliffe signed the FY2019 Audit report on behalf of PwC. The
Respondents’ statutory responsibility was to form an opinion as to whether the Bank’s
FY2019 Financial Statements showed a true and fair view and had been properly

10

prepared in accordance with the relevant financial reporting framework and the
Companies Act 2006. PwC’s report on those financial statements stated that they had
been properly prepared in accordance with International Financial Reporting
Standards and that PwC’s audit of them had been conducted in accordance with the
applicable auditing standards.
3.19. The fees for the statutory audit and related assurance services, as reported in the
FY2019 Financial Statements, were £206,000.
Events after the signing of the FY2019 Audit report
3.20. In September and October 2019, the PRA imposed requirements on the Bank to
prevent it from transacting with members of the GFG Alliance and entities introduced
by them, and to restrict the Bank's ability to accept deposits from third parties.
3.21. On 29 November 2019, PwC resigned as the Bank’s Statutory Audit Firm, citing
conflict of interest concerns.
3.22. In March 2020 the PRA varied its requirements, effectively stopping the Bank from
entering into new transactions. Also in March 2020, the Bank's Board decided to effect
a solvent wind down.
3.23. The Bank’s FY2020 financial statements (which were audited by a different firm) report
that in the year to 30 April 2020 some business introduced to the Bank by members of
the GFG Alliance was not performing as intended, resulting in a direct exposure to
GFG Alliance members. These financial statements also refer to the impacts of the
Covid-19 pandemic on the Bank and on global supply chains. A number of the Bank’s
counterparties which had originally been introduced by GFG Alliance members failed
to pay the amounts owing by them within the projected timescales. These events led
the Shareholder to provide subordinated funding to the Bank to maintain the viability of
the wind down process.
3.24. In March 2021, the PRA ordered the Bank to repay all depositors. The Bank reported
in its FY2022 financial statements that it had repaid the vast majority of customers by
30 April 2022. It made full ECL provisions against £175.6m of loans to reflect the
ongoing difficulties in collecting the remaining portfolio since FY2019.
3.25. In 2023 and 2024 the PRA took action in response to the acts and omissions of the
Bank and its CEO in 2016-2020:
3.25.1. On 4 April 2023, the PRA issued a Final Notice censuring the Bank for wide-
ranging and serious regulatory failings between 21 December 2016 and 28

11

May 2020, including breaches relating to large exposure limits, capital
reporting, governance and risk controls. The PRA indicated that it would have
imposed a fine of £8,515,000 for the breaches, but for the fact that the Bank
was in wind down and had very limited financial resources.
3.25.2. On 10 January 2024, the PRA issued a further Final Notice fining the former
Chief Executive Officer of the Bank £118,808 for failing to act with due skill,
care and diligence and failing to take reasonable steps to ensure that the
Bank had adequate systems and controls in relation to the large exposures
regime and PRA record keeping requirements, between 7 March 2016 and 28
May 2020.
4.
RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS
4.1. Rule 1 of the AEP states that Relevant Requirements has the meaning set out in
regulation 5(11) of the Statutory Auditors and Third Country Auditors Regulations 2016
(“SATCAR”). The Relevant Requirements include, but are not limited to, the
International Standards on Auditing (UK) (“ISAs”), issued by the Financial Reporting
Council and which are based on the standards issued by the International Auditing and
Assurance Standards Board.
4.2. The Relevant Requirements referred to in this Proposed Settlement Decision Notice
are the following:
4.2.1.
ISA 200 (Overall objectives of the independent auditor and the conduct of an
audit in accordance with international standards on auditing);
4.2.2.
ISA 220 (Quality Control for an Audit of Financial Statements);
4.2.3.
ISA 230 (Audit Documentation);
4.2.4.
ISA 250 (Consideration of Laws and Regulations in an Audit of Financial
Statements);
4.2.5.
ISA 315 (Identifying and Assessing the risks of Material Misstatement through
understanding the Entity and its Environment)
4.2.6.
ISA 500 (Audit Evidence);
4.2.7.
ISA 505 (External Confirmations);
4.2.8.
ISA 540 (Accounting Estimates and Related Disclosures);
4.2.9.
ISA 550 (Related Parties); and

12

4.2.10. ISA 570 (Going Concern).
4.3. The applicable versions of the ISAs are those effective for audits of financial
statements for periods ending on or after 17 June 2016, except in the case of ISA 250
and ISA 330, where the applicable versions are those effective for audits of financial
statements for periods ending on or after 15 December 2017.
4.4. Extracts from the ISAs setting out those parts which are of particular relevance to the
breaches of Relevant Requirements are provided as Appendix 1.
4.5. As Statutory Auditor, Mr Hinchliffe was responsible for the overall quality of the
FY2019 Audit and the direction, supervision, and performance of the audit in
compliance with the professional standards and applicable legal and regulatory
requirements.
4.6. As Statutory Audit Firm, PwC is responsible for any breach of Relevant Requirements
on the part of its partners or employees in the course of the FY2019 Audit.
5.
BREACHES OF RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS
Breach 1 – Audit risk assessment
Relevant ISAs
5.1. ISA 315 concerns “the auditor's responsibility to identify and assess the risks of
material misstatement in the financial statements, through understanding the entity
and its environment, including the entity's internal control” (paragraph 1).
5.2. Paragraph 5 of ISA 315 required the Respondents to perform risk assessment
procedures to provide a basis for the identification and assessment of risks of material
misstatement at the financial statement and assertion levels.
5.3. Paragraph 11 of ISA 315 required the Respondents to obtain an understanding of
various matters in relation to the Bank and its environment, including:
5.3.1.
Relevant regulatory factors and the entity's operations, ownership and
governance structures, to enable the Respondents to understand the classes
of transactions, account balances, and disclosures to be expected in the
financial statements.
5.3.2.
The Bank’s objectives and strategies, and related business risks that may
result in risks of material misstatement.

13

5.4. Paragraph 25 of ISA 315 required the Respondents to identify and assess the risks of
material misstatement at the financial statement level and the assertion level, to
provide a basis for designing and performing further audit procedures.
5.5. Paragraph 27 of ISA 315 required the Respondents to determine whether any of the
identified risks were, in their judgment, significant risks. In making that determination,
the Respondents were required to consider at least the particular matters set out in
paragraph 28 of ISA 315, which included the complexity of transactions and whether
the risk involved significant transactions with related parties.
5.6. Paragraph 31 of ISA 315 required the Respondents to revise their assessment of the
risks of material misstatement at the assertion level if they obtained audit evidence or
new information that was inconsistent with the audit evidence upon which they based
their original assessment.
5.7. The Respondents breached these requirements in a number of respects as set out
below.
Failures in the initial identification and assessment of risks
5.8. The audit team failed to give adequate consideration to the audit risks posed by the
Bank’s membership of the GFG Alliance at the planning stage of the audit:
5.8.1.
The audit team’s focus, with regard to related party transactions, was on the
disclosures required in the financial statements, and they did not adequately
consider the wider risks that related party matters posed for the audit as a
whole. The risk of material misstatement associated with related party
transactions (including those outside the ordinary course of business) is
highlighted throughout the relevant ISA, ISA 550 (for which, see Breach 3
below). Significant transactions with related parties are also highlighted as a
relevant consideration when identifying significant risks, in paragraph 28(c)
of ISA 315.
5.8.2.
The audit team was aware of the extent to which the Bank was closely
involved with other members of the GFG Alliance, by reference to the volume
and nature of the Bank’s GFG Alliance-related business and the explicit
acknowledgement in the Agenda for the Audit Planning Meeting that the main
business activities of the Bank were carried out with a view to providing
funding for members of the GFG Alliance.

14

5.8.3.
Given the level of the Bank’s business with other members of the GFG
Alliance, the audit team should have considered sources of risk arising from
this. In particular the audit team ought to have assessed the risk that, since
PwC was not the auditor of the other members of the GFG Alliance, this could
limit the ability of the audit team to understand the wider context of
transactions between members under ultimate common control.
5.8.4.
While potentially a source of risk, the Bank’s involvement with the GFG
Alliance was not the subject of specific consideration in the audit planning and
risk assessment documents. At the Audit Planning Meeting there was mention
of the fact that related party transactions posed risks, and of the need for
professional skepticism, but there was no discussion of the specific risks in
this engagement arising from the Bank’s involvement with the GFG Alliance,
or of procedures to address those risks.
5.8.5.
PwC procedures required the audit team to consider whether there were
questions regarding the integrity or conduct of the Bank's directors, senior
management or owners, or the legality of their actions. If the audit team had
researched press articles on the Bank and the Shareholder, they would have
been likely to find several articles in the year to April 2019 setting out
concerns about the “lack of financial transparency” around the GFG Alliance
that were relevant in this regard. The audit team incorrectly recorded that
there was no adverse publicity about the Bank’s owner.
5.8.6.
The wider risks around the Bank’s involvement with the GFG Alliance were
discussed and acknowledged within PwC in the context of the firm’s
subsequent resignation as auditors. They should have been appropriately
recognised and fully considered during the FY2019 Audit.
5.9. Further, the work undertaken by the audit team to update their understanding of the
Bank’s business for the purposes of the FY2019 Audit failed to identify key
developments relevant to the overall assessment of risk:
5.9.1.
The Bank's business was essentially described in the various planning
documents as invoice discounting. This did not acknowledge the diversity and
complexity of the Bank’s activities. The previous year’s 2018 Annual Report
Summary disclosed that the Bank had four separate products (receivable
finance, trade finance, inventory finance and asset finance).

15

5.9.2.
The planning documents also stated that no new contracts had been entered
into during the year. This failed to acknowledge the existence of the significant
additional loans made by the Bank.
5.9.3.
The planning documents also assumed that there were no complex customer
arrangements. It should have been apparent from the audit procedures
performed that some of the customer arrangements were indeed quite
complex, warranting particular care to understand them adequately, and the
use of audit team members with the appropriate levels of skill and experience.
When it became apparent that the Bank was undertaking transactions that
were not simple invoice discounting, the relevant contracts should have been
reviewed to properly understand the transactions and related audit risks, and
to plan how they should be addressed. However, this was not done.
5.9.4.
In that regard, paragraph 103 of the relevant Practice Note issued by the FRC
(Practice Note 19: The Audit of Banks and Building Societies in the United
Kingdom) gives as an example of “specialised activities” requiring particular
consideration when obtaining an understanding of the entity, “trade finance,
invoice discounting and factoring (where the documentation can be complex
and highly specialised)”.

financial statements to be materially misstated, is also relevant to the Respondents’
auditing of ECL.
5.86. The Respondents breached these requirements in a number of respects as set out
below.
Failure to adequately evaluate whether the “debt stacking” assumption applied by the Bank
was reasonable
5.87. It has been noted that the Bank recognised a £3.9m provision for ECL in the FY2019
Financial Statements. Management calculated this amount by the multiplication of
three factors, for each of the Bank’s loans:
5.87.1. Probability of default (“PD”) – the probability of the counterparty going into
default within the relevant period (which could be 12 months or the lifetime of
the loan, depending on whether there had been a significant increase in credit
risk since the loan was made).
5.87.2. Loss given default (“LGD”) – a measure of the loss over the total exposure if
the counterparty went into default.
5.87.3. Exposure at default – the loan balance outstanding at the point of the
borrower going into default, which was taken to be the balance as at the
reporting date.
5.88. The Bank’s approach to determining the PD and LGD for each counterparty used
models that were based on a combination of counterparty or deal specific data,
simplifying portfolio level assumptions, external data and expert judgment. For LGD,
the Bank started with a loss rate of 50% based on observable industry data, but
adjusted it downwards in the case of a number of its exposures, on the assumption
that trade receivables would rank higher than other forms of liability in the event of
default, and so would take a smaller share of the 50% loss. The rationale was that, in
the event of a loan repayment being in default, the obligor would prioritise the payment
of trade creditors in order to mitigate the risk of creditors putting the obligor into an

31

insolvency process. This “debt stacking” assumption had a significant effect on the
LGD element of the calculation, and therefore may have had a significant impact on
the ultimate ECL, although the low PDs across the portfolio limited the potential
impact.
5.89. The audit team did not appropriately evaluate and challenge this important
assumption. This was a breach of paragraphs 13(b)(ii) and 18 of ISA 540.
Failure to apply sufficient professional skepticism to other aspects of the Bank’s ECL
approach
5.90. Given the volume of business introduced by GFG Alliance members and the nature of
the Bank’s loan transactions, the audit team ought to have been more skeptical in
relation to aspects of the Bank’s approach to the calculation of ECL. The audit team
were aware of the inherent limitations of the ECL model and performed audit
procedures to conclude the ECL provision was not materially misstated. However, they
ought to have further challenged whether the specific valuation risks presented by the
structure of the loans introduced by GFG Alliance members were adequately captured
by:
5.90.1. The modelled approach to impairment adopted;
5.90.2. The use and relevance in the ECL calculations of insurance and security (the
latter being a key feature of some loan types); and
5.90.3. The lack of obligor-specific information on which to base the calculations for
multiple loan types (when the Bank should have obtained this information
under its policies and procedures on loan issuance).
5.91. The failure to properly scrutinise these matters, taken together, amounts to a failure to
apply sufficient professional skepticism in respect of the Bank’s approach to ECL, and
therefore a breach of paragraph 15 of ISA 200.
6.

6.1
Paragraph 10 of the FRC’s Sanctions Policy (Audit Enforcement Procedure) (the
“Sanctions Policy”) provides that Sanctions are intended to be effective, proportionate
and dissuasive. The reasons for imposing Sanctions are identified in paragraph 11 of
the Sanctions Policy as the following:
6.1.1. to declare and uphold proper standards of conduct amongst Statutory Auditors

32

and Statutory Audit Firms and to maintain and enhance the quality and reliability
of future audits;
6.1.2. to maintain and promote public and market confidence in Statutory Auditors
and Statutory Audit Firms and the quality of their audits and in the regulation of
the accountancy profession;
6.1.3. to protect the public from Statutory Auditors and Statutory Audit Firms whose

6.1.4. to deter Statutory Auditors and Statutory Audit Firms from breaching the
Relevant Requirements relating to Statutory Audit.
6.2. In considering the Sanctions to be imposed in this case, Executive Counsel has, in
summary, considered the following matters in accordance with the Sanctions Policy.
Nature, seriousness, gravity and duration of the breaches
6.3. The breaches of Relevant Requirements were serious and numerous. They affected a
number of different areas of the audit, although they largely stemmed from a single issue:
the failure of the audit team to properly understand the Bank’s lending and therefore the
true extent of its actual and potential exposure to GFG Alliance members. This was
compounded by the failure to appreciate and act on the escalating level of concern
expressed by the PRA about the Bank’s sustainability. The Bank's relationship with the
GFG Alliance and the terms of its lending were central to its business model, and the
failure to properly enquire into and understand those matters was very significant, in the
context of the audit.
6.4. There were a number of breaches of the Relevant Requirements in relation to
professional skepticism and obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence, which are
fundamental to the role of the independent auditor. Some of those breaches were
unrelated to the fundamental issue in relation to the audit team’s understanding of the
Bank’s business mentioned above: for example, the failure to identify the gaps in the
regulatory correspondence, to test management’s related party listing and disclosures
or to verify the existence of particular loan balances.
6.5. As a result of the breaches, the FY2019 Audit failed in its principal objective, namely to
obtain reasonable assurance about whether the FY2019 Financial Statements as a
whole were free from material misstatement. In fact, the related party disclosures note
in the FY2019 Financial Statements was materially restated in FY2020 by the addition
of £21m in outstanding loans and £7m in income, in relation to GFG Alliance members.

33

6.6. The breaches had the potential to adversely affect a significant number of people in
the United Kingdom. As at the FY2019 year-end, the Bank held £727m in customer
deposits from over 15,000 UK public savers. Of this amount, any loss to depositors up
to £657m was protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme, and would
ultimately be borne collectively by the financial services industry, which funds that
scheme. The Bank held £233m in cash, but this was only sufficient to cover
approximately a third of the deposits (a further £113m was held as other types of liquid
assets, and £434m of loans and advances).
6.7. The extent to which the sustainability of the Bank was impacted by its exposure to the
GFG Alliance, and the recoverability of loans made to GFG Alliance members, were
highly relevant to the safety of sums deposited with the Bank. Breaches in the auditing
of those matters therefore had the potential to adversely impact the depositors. In the
event, the risk of loss was averted by the intervention of the PRA and by the financial
support provided by the Shareholder in the solvent wind down of the Bank.
6.8. For those reasons, and because the Bank is a credit institution and PIE, the breaches
also had the potential to harm public confidence in the truth and fairness of financial
statements in general, and in the standards of conduct of Statutory Auditors or
Statutory Audit Firms.
6.9. Conversely:
6.9.1. The breaches were limited to one audit year;
6.9.2. They were not intentional or deliberate, reckless or dishonest;
6.9.3. They did not involve financial gain; and
6.9.4. PwC voluntarily carried out a Root Cause Analysis (“RCA”) which identified a
number of changes and improvements already implemented since the FY2019
Audit, which should reduce the likelihood of any recurrence of the breaches.
6.10. The circumstances of the Respondents are also relevant to the determination of
Sanction. PwC is (and was at the time of the FY2019 Audit) the largest audit firm in the
UK. PwC has had Sanctions imposed on it under the AEP on six previous occasions in
the last five years, and in several of those cases the breaches bore some similarity to
those in the present case (although the findings were not available to the Respondents
at the time of the FY2019 Audit).
6.11. Mr Hinchliffe has a clean disciplinary record. As an employee and Director of the firm,
his remuneration was lower than that of partners in large audit firms, who are the

34

individuals most commonly subject to Sanctions under the AEP. Although PwC has
undertaken to pay any financial sanction imposed on him, his lower level of
remuneration is still relevant in determining a proportionate figure for the sanction. This
investigation has had a significant impact on Mr Hinchliffe and was a key factor in his
decision to cease being a Statutory Auditor and to resign from PwC.
6.12. Both Respondents have accepted their responsibility for the breaches and expressed
contrition.
Identification of Sanction
6.13. Having assessed the nature, seriousness, gravity and duration of the breaches with
regard to the matters mentioned above, Executive Counsel identified the following
combination of Sanctions as appropriate:
6.13.1. Financial sanctions of £4,500,000 in the case of PwC, and £55,000 in the

6.13.2. A published statement in the form of a Severe Reprimand, in the case of each
of them.
6.13.3. A declaration that the FY2019 Audit report did not satisfy the Relevant

6.13.4. In the case of PwC, an order requiring the firm to take the following action
which is designed to prevent the recurrence of the contravention:

By 9 July 2025:
(a)
carry out an assessment of the effectiveness of additional
improvement measures identified in or as a result of the
RCA in addressing the specific shortcomings in that audit
(the relevant additional improvement measures and the
manner of the assessment having been agreed by the
FRC in advance); and
(b)
provide a report (the “Report”) which: (i) sets out the
results of the assessment, and (ii) either identifies any
further measures that PwC intends to take to address the
shortcomings, or explains why no such further measures
are necessary.

6.13.4.2.
Provide any further information or report, in connection with or
as a result of the Report, as required by the FRC.
Aggravating and mitigating factors
6.14. Executive Counsel has then taken into account any aggravating and mitigating factors
that exist, to the extent that they have not already been taken into account in relation
to the nature, seriousness, gravity and duration of the breaches.
Aggravating factors
6.15. There are no aggravating factors that have not already been considered.
Mitigating factors
6.16. All relevant mitigating factors have already been considered, except the level of co-
operation provided by the Respondents. Paragraph 69 of the Sanctions Policy explains
that, since Statutory Auditors and Statutory Audit Firms are required to co-operate with
any investigation under the AEP, only an exceptional level of co-operation will be
regarded as a mitigating factor at the point of determining Sanctions.
6.17. During the course of the investigation PwC carried out their own review of the auditing
of ECL, and the RCA in respect of the audit as a whole, and shared the results with
Executive Counsel. Having regard to the timing and impact of these steps, Executive
Counsel considers that they amount to an exceptional level of co-operation worthy of a
discount of 5% to the financial sanction. The financial sanction is therefore reduced to
£4,275,000
6.18. With regard to Mr Hinchliffe, he has shown great professionalism and resilience in
continuing to engage with the investigation in a diligent fashion. Executive Counsel
considers that, in the particular circumstances of this case, this amounts to exceptional
co-operation on his part and that a discount of 10% to the financial sanction against
him is appropriate. The financial sanction is therefore reduced to £49,500.
Deterrence
6.19. Having considered the matters set out at paragraphs 72 and 73 of the Policy,
Executive Counsel considers that no adjustment for deterrence is required in this case.

6.20. Having taken into account the full admissions by the Respondents and the stage at
which those admissions were made (at an early point within Stage 1 of the case, in
accordance with paragraph 84 of the Sanctions Policy), Executive Counsel determined

sanction against Mr Hinchliffe is further reduced to £33,412.
